prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: Across the five frames, the room is bounded by a far wall and windows roughly 3–6 m away, while clothing racks and hanging garments occupy the middle and foreground at about 0.3–2 m; the brightest region in frames 3–4 marks fabric or a rack extremely close to the camera, partly occluding the scene. A person near the left edge in frame 1 appears about 1.5–3 m away, and another person on the right in frame 5 appears roughly 1–2 m away, with the intervening racks generally between the people and the camera wearer. The sequence indicates a rightward camera turn or head sweep: left-side people and racks leave view, a close garment crosses the center, and the right-side person and window area enter view; the close fabric and possibly the camera wearer's hand are within arm's reach. Depth makes foreground-versus-background separation and the severe near-field occlusion clearer than RGB, but its smooth surfaces, blown-out bright regions, dark windows, and poorly defined human boundaries make metre estimates and distances between partly hidden objects unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The map isolates a suitcase or bag left-of-center in frame 2, people near the center-right of frame 3 and across much of frame 4, a bottle near the right side of frame 4, and a person on the right in frame 5. The frame-3 person is approximately 1–2 m ahead, while the very large frame-4 person mask implies that a person or person-like foreground region is within about 0.3–1 m; the frame-5 person is about 1–2 m away and lies to the right of the camera wearer, with the bottle above and left of that person in the preceding frame. Mask size and clipping reveal occlusion and field-of-view changes: the suitcase is partly fragmented, the frame-4 person extends beyond the top and lower image boundaries, and the frame-5 person is cut off below the torso; together these changes match a rightward turn past nearby racks and people. Segmentation makes object identity, silhouette, overlap, and partial visibility clearer than RGB, but it misses most racks and garments, labels only scattered instances, and the enormous frame-4 person mask appears unreliable because RGB mainly shows very close fabric and partial body-like shapes there.
descriptions.pose: Pose detects only sparse anatomy: a small upright body or arm-like skeleton left-of-center in frame 2, and a hand cluster above a horizontal shoulder-or-arm segment on the right in frame 5; frames 1, 3, and 4 contain no reliable skeletons. The frame-2 detection is roughly 2–3 m ahead and left of the camera wearer, whereas the frame-5 hand and upper-body points are roughly 1–2 m ahead on the right, with the hand above the torso line and potentially within that person's own arm reach but probably outside the camera wearer's arm reach. The detections shift from left to right across the sequence as the viewpoint turns, but missing joints prevent a dependable estimate of whether either person faces or looks toward the camera wearer, and no person-to-person spacing can be recovered confidently. Pose can expose joint locations and limb orientation that motion blur obscures in RGB, but here heavy occlusion, truncation, blur, and likely false or incomplete keypoints make body orientation, gaze, approach, retreat, and hand proximity especially unreliable.
